headline: Support Group Forms for People 'Jumpscared by Their Own Reflection'
subheadline: Weekly meetings held in rooms with no mirrors; attendance exceeds expectations
summary: A support group for people who have been startled by their own reflection has resonated with thousands.
content:
A support group for people who have experienced the phenomenon of being "jumpscared by their own reflection" has grown from a Threadit joke to a legitimate weekly meeting with chapters in 47 cities.

"It happens more than people admit," said group founder Marcus Chen at a recent meeting held in a carefully mirror-free community center. "You walk past a window, catch a glimpse of movement, your heart stops—and then you realize it's you. The shame is real. The fear is real. We're here to process both."

The group, called "Reflectors Anonymous," provides a judgment-free space for members to share their experiences. Stories range from bathroom mirror incidents to catching unexpected glimpses in car windows to the dreaded "walked past a dark TV screen."

"The worst one for me was a storefront window at night," shared one member. "I saw a figure approaching and prepared to cross the street. Then I realized the figure was mimicking my exact movements. It was me. I had prepared to flee from myself."

The phenomenon, which psychologists call "autoscopic startle response," is surprisingly common. A recent survey found that 84.7% of respondents had been startled by their own reflection at least once, with 23% reporting it happens "regularly."

"We don't recognize ourselves as quickly as we think," explained Dr. Patricia Huang, who has consulted with the group. "There's a processing delay. In that delay, we see a stranger. And strangers in mirrors are inherently alarming."

The group has developed coping strategies, including "mirror anticipation exercises" and "reflective surface awareness training." They've also created a hotline for acute incidents.

"Sometimes you just need to call someone and say 'I saw myself in a spoon and screamed,'" explained Chen. "And have someone respond with 'I understand. You're not alone.'"

Membership has reached 8,470. Their motto: "We see you. Even when you don't see you."
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
